talks.title: How to Contact the ISS with a $30 Radio
talks.teaser: Gregg Horton demonstrates tracking orbital passes and making two-way amateur radio contacts with the International Space Station using budget handheld radios.
talks.summary:
In this presentation at the DEF CON 29 Ham Radio Village, Gregg Horton (K6XSS) presents an accessible, beginner-friendly guide to establishing amateur radio contact with the International Space Station (ISS) using an inexpensive handheld transceiver. He opens at 03:00 by dispelling the belief that amateur radio requires costly equipment, explaining that high-frequency satellite communication can be accomplished with a basic thirty-dollar handheld radio like the Baofeng UV-5R.

Gregg explains the operation of the amateur radio cross-band repeater aboard the ISS at 06:00, detailing how low-Earth orbit satellites receive VHF signals and retransmit them across vast geographic footprints. At 09:00, he showcases decoding Slow Scan Television (SSTV) image transmissions broadcast by Russian cosmonauts during special commemoration events using free audio demodulation apps on smartphones.

Walking through orbital dynamics at 12:00, Gregg demonstrates how to use mobile satellite tracking tools to identify pass windows and antenna elevation angles during the typical nine-minute transit window. He details programming standard VHF uplink (145.990 MHz) and UHF downlink (437.800 MHz) frequencies with required CTCSS tones at 15:00, and explains compensating for orbital Doppler shift at 18:00. He concludes at 21:00 by encouraging amateur radio operators to expand their experimentation to amateur cubesats and orbital repeaters. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Getting Started with Low Power / Long Distance Comms
talks.teaser: Eric Escobar shares foundational techniques for low-power (QRP) and long-range RF communications, leveraging LoRa, directional antennas, and digital protocols.
talks.summary:
Eric Escobar provides a practical, beginner-friendly introduction to low-power, long-range radio communications (QRP) at the Ham Radio Village, demonstrating how amateur operators can transmit signals over hundreds or thousands of miles using minimal electrical power.

[06:06] Escobar explains the physics of radio frequency propagation across High Frequency (HF) bands, detailing how ionospheric refraction (skywave propagation) enables signals to bounce beyond the horizon and circumvent the curvature of the earth. He compares traditional voice modes with highly efficient digital protocols like FT8 and JS8Call, which can decode transmissions buried beneath the atmospheric noise floor with as little as five watts of power.

[11:53] The presentation examines essential portable hardware and antenna kits, highlighting portable deployment setups such as the Chameleon MPAS 2.0 modular antenna system. Escobar discusses the trade-offs of end-fed half-wave (EFHW) wires, random wire antennas, and magnetic loop antennas. He touches on emerging low-power decentralized mesh networks like LoRa/Meshtastic [18:06], providing guidance on off-grid battery management, solar charging, and field emergency communication planning.

talks.title: Amateur Radio Digital Modes Primer
talks.teaser: Jon Marler breaks down modern amateur radio digital modes (FT8, JS8Call, APRS), demonstrating keyboard-to-keyboard data transmission over high frequencies.
talks.summary:
In this comprehensive tutorial at the DEF CON 29 Ham Radio Village, Jon Marler (K4CHN) delivers an introductory guide to amateur radio digital communication modes, exploring the hardware, software, and protocols used for text and image transmissions. He opens at 09:00 by contrasting soundcard-based digital modes with digital voice repeaters and hotspots, explaining the distinct equipment requirements for each operating style.

Jon demonstrates keyboard-to-keyboard conversational modes like PSK31 and continuous wave (CW) at 18:00, highlighting their spectral efficiency and weak-signal resilience under poor atmospheric conditions. At 27:00, he examines Slow Scan Television (SSTV), demonstrating automated reception and image decoding workflows for terrestrial and satellite image broadcasts.

Diving into low-cost station building at 36:00, Jon explains how to build custom audio interfaces using inexpensive USB soundcards and Anderson Powerpole connectors to link transceivers to computers. He demonstrates portable decoding setups using iOS and Android devices at 45:00, before discussing WSJT-X configuration for weak-signal modes like FT8. He concludes at 56:00 by welcoming attendees to connect in person at the Ham Radio Village to test their digital rigs. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)
